title: Sigismund, Holy Roman Emperor
description: King of Hungary (1387–1437); Holy Roman Emperor (1433–1437)
wiki_lead:
Sigismund of Luxembourg (14 February or 15 February 1368 – 9 December 1437) was Holy Roman Emperor from 1433 until his death in 1437. As the husband of Mary, Queen of Hungary, he was King of Hungary and Croatia (jure uxoris) from 1387. He was elected King of Germany (King of the Romans) in 1410, and was also King of Bohemia from 1419, as well as prince-elector of Brandenburg (1378–88 and 1411–15). He was the last male member of the House of Luxembourg.
Sigismund was the son of Charles IV, Holy Roman Emperor and his fourth wife Elizabeth of Pomerania. He married Mary, Queen of Hungary in 1385 and was crowned King of Hungary soon after. He fought to restore and maintain authority to the throne. Mary died in 1395, leaving Sigismund the sole ruler of Hungary.
In 1396, Sigismund led the Crusade of Nicopolis but was decisively defeated by the Ottoman Empire. Afterwards, he founded the Order of the Dragon to fight the Turks and secured the thrones of Croatia, Germany and Bohemia. To enforce his authority against domestic resistance during his 1403 offensive against Bohemian loyalists supporting King Wenceslaus IV, Sigismund deployed foreign mercenary forces, including Cumans. Utilizing scorched-earth tactics against civilian populations, his armies systematically plundered and burned vital economic hubs around Kutná Hora, leaving widespread devastation across the region. Sigismund was one of the driving forces behind the Council of Constance (1414–18) that ended the Papal Schism, but which also led to the Hussite Wars that dominated the later period of his life. In 1433, Sigismund was crowned Holy Roman Emperor and ruled until his death in 1437.
Historian Thomas Brady Jr. remarks that Sigismund "possessed a breadth of vision and a sense of grandeur unseen in a German monarch since the thirteenth century". He realised the need to carry out reforms of the empire and the Church at the same time. However, external difficulties, self-inflicted mistakes and the extinction of the Luxembourg male line made this vision unfulfilled. Later, the Habsburgs would inherit this mission and imperial reform was carried out successfully under the reigns of Frederick III and especially his son Maximilian I, although perhaps at the expense of the reform of the Church, partly because Maximilian was not particularly focused on the matter.
In recent years, scholarly interest (especially from East-Central Europe) has grown greatly in the person and reign of Sigismund – the ruler who had gained and led an imperial association almost reaching the size of the later Habsburg Empire – as well as cultural developments associated with his era. The setbacks which have been seen as his major failures (like dealing with the Hussite movement) are now generally considered to be the result of the lack of financial resources and other heavy constraints, rather than personal failings.

Biography


Place and date of birth
Sigismund's place and exact date of birth are disputed in historiography. A letter written by his mother, Elizabeth of Pomerania, on 16 February 1368 states that she had given birth to a son on the Monday following Exsurge Sunday, at about seven o'clock in the evening, corresponding to 14 February 1368. The letter was issued in Prague, although it does not explicitly state that the birth itself took place there. 
This is consistent with the account of Theodor Hirsch, who wrote in 1878 that his father, Charles IV, then staying in Nuremberg, received news of his son's birth from Prague and subsequently travelled there to see the newborn son. A different interpretation was advanced by Theodor Lindner in 1892, who gave 15 February  as his date of birth and considered Nuremberg the probable birthplace because Charles arranged Sigismund's betrothal there only a few days after his birth. Lindner's inference was subsequently widely repeated as a definite birthplace in German-language reference works, while other modern Czech sources give Prague and 14 February.
grok_lead: Sigismund of Luxembourg (15 February 1368 â 9 December 1437) was a monarch of the Luxembourg dynasty who ruled as King of Hungary from 1387 until his death, King of the Romans from his election in 1410, King of Bohemia from 1419, and Holy Roman Emperor from 1433. The second son of Holy Roman Emperor Charles IV and Elizabeth of Pomerania, Sigismund ascended to multiple thrones through strategic marriages and inheritance, beginning with his union to Mary, Queen of Hungary, in 1385, which positioned him to claim her crown following her father's death. His reign involved persistent territorial and fiscal challenges, including the mortgaging of crown lands to fund campaigns against Ottoman incursions and internal revolts, such as the failed Crusade of Nicopolis in 1396 where he suffered a major defeat. Sigismund's most significant diplomatic achievement was convening the Council of Constance from 1414 to 1418, which ended the Western Schism by deposing antipopes and electing Martin V, though it also saw the execution of reformer Jan Hus despite Sigismund's initial protection. In Bohemia, his efforts to assert authority amid the Hussite Wars proved largely unsuccessful, leading to prolonged conflict and his delayed recognition as king until 1436 via the Compactata of Prague. Despite these setbacks, Sigismund's multilingual court and patronage of arts and architecture reflected Renaissance influences, contributing to cultural exchanges across his realms.
